processes.description: A trader, scheduler or pipeline contact asks the data or facility team to set up new pooling, storage or delivery points and combinations, re-map a zone, change a pipe code, zero confirmed nominations or remove meters from an estimate. The facility team enters the change in Global Facilities or the scheduling system, sometimes only after authorization from the desk lead, and confirms it back, often naming who is assigned the meter. Some rounds need extra data gathered first, such as State and County details for a list of meters.
steps: A requester emails a list of points, meters or mappings to create, change or retire.
Missing reference data, such as State and County for listed meters, is gathered from colleagues.
Where needed, the change is authorized by the responsible desk lead.
The facility team sets up or changes the record in Global Facilities or the scheduling system.
Related records are adjusted, such as deferred delivery points, nominations or estimates.
The team confirms the set-up and names the person assigned to the meter.

stalls.summary: A forwarded spreadsheet of meters arrived without clear instructions, and the recipient could not tell what was being asked before passing it on for State and County details.

automation.approach: A standard set-up request form capturing point type, pipeline, zone, mapping, State and County, effective date and approver, validated against the facility master before entry, with an automatic confirmation naming the assigned scheduler.
automation.rationale: Requests arrive as free-text lists of differing shape and sometimes lack the data needed to set up a point. A fixed request layout gets complete, approved requests to the facility team the first time and makes entry largely mechanical.

work_estimate.rationale: Entering a few points or mappings in the facility system, checking the related contracts or nominations, and occasionally looking up location data for a meter list takes roughly a quarter to half an hour; larger lists take longer. Validation and data entry from a structured form could be largely tooled; approval and exceptions stay manual.

processes.description: Staff or facilities announce a move and pass on packing and labeling instructions from the move packets, such as tagging chairs with wire tags. Individuals reply with timing preferences and how much they have to move, and coordinators ask facilities to move equipment such as flat screens on a set morning, chasing when the work has not happened.
steps: Facilities or an assistant circulates the move date and packing and labeling instructions.
Staff pack and label boxes, chairs and equipment.
Staff reply with timing preferences and the size of their move.
A coordinator asks facilities to move specific equipment at a set time.
The coordinator follows up when the move has not been carried out.

stalls.summary: A requested equipment move was promised early in the week and still had not been done days later, so the coordinator had to chase facilities.

automation.approach: A move checklist sent with the packet listing labeling, packing, equipment and timing items, with a facilities ticket per equipment move that carries a promised date and triggers a reminder when it passes.
automation.rationale: The work is packing and labeling by individuals plus scheduling with facilities; a checklist keeps instructions in one place, and tracked requests replace manual chasing.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is packing a few boxes, labeling chairs and equipment, and arranging a slot with facilities; the quotes show small moves, so a short block per round. Physical packing cannot be tooled; only scheduling and reminders could be.

processes.description: Users report errors in operations and trading systems: bridge-back errors on meters for a production month, bad numbers in POPS, failed scrapes, Unify database hangs, duplicate Sitara deals and position manager faults. Support or IT investigates and fixes them, while IT also announces outages, releases, URL and server changes and EOL rollouts, sometimes with steps users must take such as rebooting or mapping a drive. Users collect enhancement requests and confirm releases look right from the commercial side.
steps: A user notices an error, such as a bridge-back error, bad volumes or a failed import, and reports it with the meter, deal or date.
Support investigates the cause in the affected system.
Data is corrected, such as killing a duplicate Sitara deal or re-running a bridge.
IT announces outages, releases or configuration changes and any user action needed.
Users test or confirm the fix or release and report remaining issues.
Recurring problems are listed as enhancement requests for later releases.

stalls.summary: Bridges between systems keep erroring out, leaving meters and months unbridged until someone corrects them by hand.
System outages and bad data after restarts disrupt operations, such as wrong POPS numbers after TDS was taken down, a Unify database hang and a scrape down through a night shift.
Fixes wait on release cycles: a missing curve in the latest version is held until a code freeze lifts, and access problems persist after a cluster is not reconfigured.
Desktop tools fail in ways users must diagnose themselves, such as a browser error on import caused by an unmapped drive, and a position manager that is not working.

automation.approach: Automated monitoring of bridge jobs and scrapes that flags failed meters, deals and runs to the owning team, a single outage and release calendar with required user actions, and a known-issues guide for common desktop errors.
automation.rationale: Much of the hands-on time goes to spotting and correcting recurring bridge errors and diagnosing known desktop faults. A written procedure for triage and correction, backed by exception reports, shortens each round and routes issues to the right owner.

work_estimate.rationale: A typical round is diagnosing one error, such as a bridge-back failure or bad volumes, checking the affected deal or meter and correcting it, or testing a release; roughly half an hour, longer for outages that require re-checking data. Detection and routing of bridge failures could be tooled; diagnosis and fixes stay manual.
